place: A shallow rocky stream at the edge of a forest, current gentle, water cold and clear.
lines: fill my boots with water
carry it back to camp
outcome: Boots are not sealed containers, so water poured in sloshes straight back out through the laces and seams with every step. Only a trickle survives the walk to camp, and the player's feet and socks end up soaked in the meantime. The wet leather rubs against skin as it walks, raising a blister within an hour or two. A half-work: some water was moved, most was not, and a minor injury came free.

place: A steep dirt path switchbacking up from a well to a hilltop camp, loose gravel underfoot.
lines: fill the bucket at the well
carry it up to camp
outcome: The bucket fills fine and starts the climb full, but the path is steep and loose. Partway up a foot slips on gravel and the bucket lurches, throwing out a good fraction of the water at once; the rest keeps sloshing out over an open rim with every uneven stride for the remaining climb. Only a partial amount reaches camp, and the player has to consider a second trip.

place: A dry, sun-baked ridge campsite in midsummer, a waterskin left on a flat rock in direct sun.
lines: leave the waterskin open on the rock, I'll be back later
outcome: Left uncapped in direct sun for hours, the waterskin loses water steadily to the heat and dry air even though nothing visibly happens to it. By the time the player checks back, the skin holds noticeably less than was left, and a faint pale mineral ring has formed at the old waterline where dissolved minerals stayed behind as the water they were part of left. Nobody did anything more after walking away; the loss just accrued.

place: A camp pitched in a shallow hollow beside a dry streambed, tents low to the ground, no drainage dug.
outcome: Heavy rain falls overnight while everyone sleeps. The dry streambed the camp sits beside fills fast and its rising water spills past its old bank into the hollow the camp occupies. By dawn the tent floor is standing in a couple of inches of water and the bedding is soaked through; nobody noticed anything happen, only its result. The soaked bedding takes most of the next day to dry out in the sun, and smells of mildew afterward regardless.

Left alone, the sediment slowly resettles; drawn or drunk too soon, the water carries stirred-up mud and whatever was living in that mud with it.

place: A slow, waist-deep river crossing point, banks lined with fallen logs and loose stones.
lines: lash some logs together with rope

outcome: The lashed logs float fine on their own. Loaded with a stack of stones to ferry across, the raft sits lower and lower in the water as weight is added; partway across the river its waterline reaches the tops of the logs and buoyancy simply runs out. The raft goes under, dumping the stones to the riverbed and leaving the player soaked and wading the rest of the way. It floats when light and sinks when it does not have enough of itself above water to carry the load.

An adult nearby hears the splash and shouting, lowers a second rope, and hauls the child out soaked and frightened but unhurt. It was a close thing that depended entirely on someone being within earshot.

outcome: Dipping and smearing the rope through the warm tar coats it evenly. While still warm the tar stays gummy, transferring onto the player's hands and anything else it touches. Left to cool for a good while, the tar hardens and the rope turns stiff and water-resistant, useful for outdoor rigging. Handling it before it has cooled is what makes the mess, not the tarring itself.

place: A stream bank near camp, a shirt stained with dried mud and old blood from a scraped knee, no soap on hand.
lines: wash the blood and mud out of my shirt in the stream
outcome: Plain running water and scrubbing lift the mud well, since it was only loose particles never bound to the fibers. The blood is a different matter: dried and set into the weave, it only lightens to a dull brown shadow under water alone, since nothing breaks down a set protein stain without soap. The shirt comes out cleaner, not clean; the stain would have needed soap, or a rinse before it ever dried.

place: A hearth-side workspace: rendered fat saved from cooking, a barrel of wood ash and rainwater, a big pot.

outcome: Water passed slowly through wood ash pulls its alkaline salts out into a sharp, slippery lye. Mixed with rendered fat and heated, the two react into a thick, cloudy paste that resembles neither ingredient it came from. Left to cool and sit for days in a mold, the paste firms from soft to a hard bar that can actually lift grease and dirt, unlike either ash or fat alone.

place: A smokehouse shed, strips of meat laid out with a small sack of salt, humid weather outside.
lines: rub salt on the meat to keep it from spoiling
outcome: Salt rubbed over the meat draws moisture out and slows the bacteria that cause spoiling, but only where it actually reaches. The coat is thin and uneven, and the shed sits humid rather than dry, so the meat never fully dries out either. A few days on, the well-salted outer parts hold up fine, but a damp patch under a fold where the salt never reached starts to smell and discolor: it spoils anyway, and has to be cut away before the rest is trusted.

place: A storeroom shelf where an iron pot sits half-full of leftover brine from preserving vegetables, forgotten for days.
outcome: Salty water left standing in an iron pot is far harder on the metal than plain water, since dissolved salt speeds the same rusting that rain causes elsewhere, working from the inside where nobody is looking. Over several days the rust eats through a weak spot at the pot's bottom seam. The brine slowly seeps out through the new pinhole, leaving a crusty salt-and-rust stain on the shelf and, eventually, an empty pot with a hole in it.
